newsitem.title: IRAQ: No New Year reprieve for impoverished Iraqis.
newsitem.headline: No New Year reprieve for impoverished Iraqis.

text.p: Iraqis relying on food rations for more than six years will have to wait a little longer before seeing the fruits of Baghdad's newly implemented oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.
There was no change in the amount of rations for January listed in a government announcement printed in official newspapers on Monday.
Officials have promised to increase the rations after the implementation of the U.N. deal but cautioned that it would take some time to sell the oil and buy the food.

Iraq started limited oil exports three weeks ago. Under the pact Baghdad is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil every six months to buy food and medicine for the Iraqi population, suffering from stringent trade sanctions imposed after Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Officials have not said when the food will arrive.
Each Iraqi is currently entitled to 1.25 kg (2.75 lb) of rice, seven kg (15.4 lb) of flour, 500 grams (1.1 lb) of sugar, 750 grams (1.6 lb) of cooking oil and 100 grams of tea every month.
These items are sold by the government at giveaway prices.

Traders and money dealers in Baghdad said that the Iraqi currency slipped slightly against the dollar on Monday because there was no increase in rations in the announcement carried by newspapers which asked retailers to collect supplies of the rationed goods from Trade Ministry warehouses for distribution.
The dinar was trading at 1,200 to the dollar, compared to 1,100 on Sunday.
Reflecting the drop in the value of the dinar, the price of some goods went up in the open market.
A kg of sugar sold for 600 dinars, up from 500 on Sunday, and a kg of tea went up to 1,600 dinars from 1,200.
The start of oil exports had initially more than doubled the value of the dinar to a high of 700 to the dollar from 1,650.

Iraqi Trade Minister Mohammed Mehdi Saleh was quoted by newspapers earlier this month as saying once food reached Iraq, the monthly rice ration would be raised to 2.5 kg (5.5 lb), flour to nine kg (20 lb) and sugar to two kg (4.4 lb). Baby formula, tea and soap rations also go up.
Iraqi media have reported the Trade Ministry signing several food deals with foreign firms since Iraqi oil exports began.
A Jordanian delegation is in Baghdad trying to win contracts to supply Iraq with commodities allowed by the oil deal.
